title: A Covenant to Put Away Foreign Wives
summary: As Ezra prays and weeps before the temple, a large crowd gathers and weeps with him. Shecaniah proposes that the people make a covenant to send away their foreign wives and children, and Ezra has the leaders swear to do it. All the men of Judah and Benjamin assemble in the rain, confess, and agree to a process of hearings town by town, with only a few objecting. Over three months the cases are examined, and the book ends with a list of the priests, Levites, and laymen who had married foreign women.
story: Chapter 9 ended with Ezra's prayer and no request, only the confession that no one could stand before God. Chapter 10 shows the community responding. The initiative comes not from Ezra but from a layman, Shecaniah, and from the people themselves, who weep with Ezra and ask him to act. The chapter moves from prayer to covenant to public assembly to a careful legal process, and the book of Ezra ends abruptly with a list of names. There is no celebration and no summary. The story of the returned community continues in Nehemiah, where the same problem appears again (Nehemiah 13:23-27), a sign that the reform of Ezra 10 did not settle the matter for good.
historical:
The assembly met on the twentieth day of the ninth month (Kislev, in November or December), probably in 458 BC on the traditional dating, about four and a half months after Ezra's arrival. That was the season of winter rain in Judah, which explains the people's trembling in verse 9 and their request in verse 13 that the matter be handled by local hearings rather than in the open square. The hearings ran from the first day of the tenth month to the first day of the first month of the following year, about three months.

Jehohanan son of Eliashib, in whose chamber Ezra fasted (verse 6), has played a part in the debate about the dates of Ezra and Nehemiah. A Johanan appears among the descendants of the high priest Eliashib, Nehemiah's contemporary (Nehemiah 12:22-23), and a high priest named Johanan is mentioned in the Elephantine papyri in 407 BC. Scholars who date Ezra after Nehemiah think this is the same man; others note that both names were common and that the chamber may simply have been named after an earlier Jehohanan. The list in verses 18-43 names a little over a hundred men, including seventeen priests, some from the high priest's own family.
cultural:
An oath or covenant in the ancient world was a binding commitment made before God, and breaking it invited his judgment. By having the leaders swear an oath, Ezra made the reform a public, collective obligation rather than a private opinion. The penalty for failing to appear (verse 8) combined two things the community took seriously: forfeiture of property, which meant loss of livelihood, and expulsion from the assembly of the exiles, which meant loss of membership in the people of God.

Sending away a wife was the language of divorce, which Deuteronomy 24:1-4 allowed and regulated. A divorced wife in the ancient Near East normally returned to her father's household, and in many cases she would take her dowry with her. Children, especially young ones, often stayed with their mothers. The text says little about how the women and children were provided for, and the silence is one of the chapter's painful features. The guilt offering of a ram presented by the priests (verse 19) followed the law for those who had committed a breach of faith concerning holy things (Leviticus 5:14-19).
literary: The chapter has two unequal parts: a narrative of the covenant and assembly (verses 1-17) and a list of the men involved (verses 18-44). The narrative shifts from the first person of chapter 9 to the third person, speaking of Ezra by name. It uses the vocabulary of the earlier chapters: unfaithfulness, separation, trembling at God's word, the assembly of the exiles. The dialogue is vivid, especially Shecaniah's speech, which moves from confession to hope to a call to action: there is hope for Israel in spite of this. Verse 15 is ambiguous in Hebrew: it may say that four men opposed the plan, or that they supervised it; most modern translations, including the BSB, read opposition. The book ends with its last verse awkwardly phrased in Hebrew; the Greek book 1 Esdras reads that the men sent the women away with their children, and English translations vary.

outline.t: The people weep, and Shecaniah proposes a covenant
The oath, Ezra's fast, and the summons to assemble
The assembly in the rain agrees to a process
Priests, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers involved

doctrines.note: The people move from weeping to confession to concrete action, and Shecaniah declares there is hope for Israel even after unfaithfulness. The chapter shows repentance as more than feeling: it is a costly change of direction. It also shows how painful and contested such change can be.
The people make a covenant before God to put right what they believe has breached their covenant with him. The reform is understood as a return to covenant loyalty, grounded in the law.

Separation from the peoples of the land is presented as necessary to preserve Israel's distinct life with God. The chapter raises the hard question of how holiness is pursued, and later Scripture shapes the answer in new ways (see the hard question below).

words.note: Miqveh, hope. Shecaniah says there is hope for Israel in spite of this (verse 2). The word is rare, used also in Jeremiah 14:8 and 17:13, where God himself is called the hope of Israel. After Ezra's prayer of utter guilt, it is a layman who names hope.

Nokri, foreign, used seven times in the chapter. It describes someone from outside the community, and it is the word used of Solomon's foreign wives (1 Kings 11:1). Ruth, too, calls herself a foreigner (Ruth 2:10), yet she joins Israel by committing to its God, which shows that the word describes status, not destiny.

Badal, to separate. Ezra calls the people to separate themselves from the peoples of the land and from their foreign wives (verse 11). In Ezra 6:21 the same verb described outsiders who separated themselves from uncleanness to join Israel. The word always implies separating from something toward God.

Maal, to be unfaithful, the verb form of the key word of chapter 9. It is used of treachery against God, of breaking faith in marriage, and of misusing holy things. Shecaniah and Ezra both use it to name what has happened (verses 2 and 10).

christ: The chapter shows a community trying to keep its faithfulness to God pure at great human cost, and it ends without resolution. The New Testament takes up the same concern for a holy people but reshapes how that holiness is guarded. Paul tells believers married to unbelievers not to divorce them if the unbelieving spouse is willing to stay, because the unbelieving partner is made holy through the believer and the children are holy (1 Corinthians 7:12-14). In Christ the direction of holiness is reversed: it spreads outward instead of being threatened by contact. Jesus himself touched the unclean without becoming unclean, and his people are called to be holy in the world rather than to withdraw from it. The link is a development across the canon: Ezra 10 shows the seriousness of covenant faithfulness, and the gospel shows how God makes a holy people from those once far off (Ephesians 2:13).

hard.q: How should we understand a reform that sent away wives and children?
hard.a:
This is one of the most troubling scenes in the Old Testament. Women and children who had done nothing wrong themselves were sent away, and the text says nothing about their fate. Malachi, probably from the same period, condemns divorce and faithlessness to the wife of one's youth (Malachi 2:14-16), and the New Testament tells believers not to divorce unbelieving spouses (1 Corinthians 7:12-14).

Interpreters respond in different ways. Some read the reform as a tragic but necessary measure at a moment when the small community was in real danger of being absorbed into the religions around it, as the northern kingdom had been, so that nothing would be left of the people through whom God's promises were to come. They note that the women's households were linked to abominations, that the law of Deuteronomy 7 forbade such marriages, and that the cases were examined one by one rather than handled by decree. Others hold that the narrative describes what happened without holding it up as a model for all times, and that later Scripture (Ruth, Isaiah 56, Malachi, and the New Testament) points to a different answer. Some combine the two views: the reform was a real act of repentance within the old covenant, but it cannot be applied directly to Christians, whose calling in mixed marriages is set out by Paul. All agree that the passage should never be used to justify ethnic exclusion, since the Bible's concern here is faithfulness to God.

questions: Shecaniah said there was hope for Israel in the same breath as confessing unfaithfulness. How can a community hold honest confession and real hope together?
The reform was costly and some people opposed it. How do you discern when a painful change is faithfulness to God and when it is harshness?
Paul later taught believers married to unbelievers not to leave them. What does that teaching suggest about how holiness works under the new covenant?
